Common questions

What is an electronic press kit (EPK)?

A one-page summary a musician or band sends to venues, festivals, playlisters, and press — bio, photo, streaming/social links, upcoming shows, and any press coverage — so a booker or writer can evaluate the act without a back-and-forth email. More background: what belongs in an EPK, and what doesn't.

Is this free, and do I need an account?

Yes, and no. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is stored anywhere but your own browser. Fill in the form and download the result — there is no account, no watermark, and no upsell.

Where does my photo come from?

You paste a link to a photo you already host somewhere (your own site, an Instagram post, a public Google Drive/Dropbox link, an image host). This tool does not accept file uploads, so nothing you have not already made public ever leaves your device.

What do I do with the generated file?

Download the HTML file and host it anywhere (your own site, GitHub Pages, or just attach it to an email), or copy the plain-text version straight into an email or a festival submission form.

Why not just build one myself in a document editor?

You can — see this generator vs. assembling one by hand for what a blank document does and doesn't catch.

Applying for a day job between shows? The ATS resume checker is the same job for a different gatekeeper — it checks a resume's format survives an applicant tracking system the way this builds the one-pager a venue or blog actually asks for.

Pitching brands instead of venues? The media kit generator is the same job one step further along — it builds the sponsorship one-pager a content creator sends a brand, with reach, audience, and rate-card fields instead of streaming links and tour dates.

EPK Generator vs. assembling one by hand in a document editor

A word processor or slide deck can hold the same bio, links, tour dates, and press quotes this generator does — most press kits ever sent were built exactly that way. What it does not do on its own: flag a missing booking email, keep a plain-text copy in sync with the formatted one every time you edit it, or lay out the page. This tool does all three the moment the form is filled in.

What each approach actually does

A document editor — a word processor, a slide deck, a blank page in any general-purpose tool — will hold anything you type: bio, streaming and social links, tour dates, press quotes, a photo. Nothing about the blank page tells you what a press kit is expected to include, so a kit missing a booking contact, or with no way to actually hear the music, ships exactly as easily as a complete one. Producing a plain-text version for a submission form that rejects attachments means building a second copy and manually keeping it matching every time the formatted one changes. Layout — type sizes, spacing, where the photo sits relative to the bio — is a design decision you make yourself, each time you revise it.

This generator takes the same content through one form and builds both files at once: a self-contained, print-friendly HTML one-sheet and a plain-text edition, generated from the identical data so the two can never drift apart. Before it builds anything it requires an artist name and a bio; separately, without blocking generation, it warns when there is no booking contact email, no streaming or social link, or no photo link — the specific gaps a booker or blog notices first, not a spelling or grammar check. The form autosaves to your own browser as you type, so closing the tab mid-edit does not lose the draft.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I forgot to include a way to actually contact me.This generator — warns before you send the kit out, not after a booker gives up.
A festival form won't take an attachment; I need plain text.This generator — built from the same data, every time, so it never falls out of sync.
I want full control over layout, typography, and a custom design.A document editor or design tool — this generator uses one fixed template, deliberately.
I closed the tab halfway through filling in the form.This generator — the draft autosaves locally and reloads where you left off.
What actually belongs in a press kit in the first place?This generator's own explanation of what an EPK is and isn't.
Is my content uploaded anywhere either way?No, with this generator — everything runs in your browser. A document editor's own upload behavior depends on which one you use.

The two are not mutually exclusive: a document editor is still the right tool for a kit built around custom design work a fixed template cannot express. For the common case — a complete, correctly-formatted one-pager and a plain-text edition to send tonight, with the obvious gaps flagged before a booker finds them — filling in a form is faster than laying out a page.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the generator runs in your browser, and it keeps working with the connection off once loaded.

Common questions

Can I just build a press kit in a word processor or slide deck myself?

Yes — a document editor holds the same bio, links, tour dates, and quotes this generator does, and plenty of press kits in circulation were built exactly that way. What it does not do on its own is tell you the kit is missing something a booker expects, produce a plain-text copy alongside the formatted one, or lay out the page — all three are on you, every time you update it.

What does the generator check that a blank document does not?

A blank document accepts whatever you type and stays silent about what you left out. This generator requires an artist name and a bio before it will build anything, and separately warns — without blocking — when there is no booking contact email, no streaming or social link, or no photo link, because those are the specific gaps a booker or blog notices first.

Why does a plain-text version matter?

Plenty of festival submission forms and booking emails reject an attached file or strip its formatting, and a document built in a word processor or slide tool has no plain-text edition unless you build one separately and then keep it matching every time you update the original. This generator produces both from the same form in the same pass, so the two never drift apart.

Is a document editor ever the better choice?

Yes, for a layout this generator does not offer — a designed multi-page PDF with custom typography and photo placement, or a kit built around a visual identity a document or design tool can express and this one, deliberately kept to one plain template, cannot. This generator trades that design flexibility for a page that appears the moment the form is filled in, with no layout decisions to make.

what-is-an-epk.html.text:
← Back to the EPK generator

What is an electronic press kit, and what belongs in it?

An electronic press kit (EPK) is a one-page summary a musician or band sends to the people who decide whether to book, cover, or playlist them — a venue talent buyer, a festival submission reviewer, a blog or playlist curator, a radio music director. It exists because that person is almost always looking at dozens or hundreds of submissions and deciding fast: who is this, what do they sound like, what have they done, and how do I reach them.

What belongs in it

  • A short bio — a few sentences to two short paragraphs. Lead with what you sound like and any concrete, checkable facts (years active, notable shows, releases) before adjectives.
  • One good photo — a live shot or a clean promo photo. It does not need to be a professional shoot to start.
  • Links to actually listen — Spotify, Bandcamp, YouTube, whatever is live. This is the section a reviewer clicks first.
  • Contact info — a booking or press email a reader can use without hunting through a website.
  • Upcoming shows, if any — proves you're active and gives a reader a reason to feature you now.
  • Press quotes, if you have any — even one line from a local blog is social proof. Skip this section entirely until you do; a placeholder quote reads worse than none.

What doesn't belong in it

Your whole discography, a mission statement, or anything a reader has to scroll far to get past. An EPK is a fast decision aid, not a website — if you want the deeper version, link to your actual site from it, not the other way around.

How it differs from a website or an Instagram bio

A website is built for fans and can be as deep as you like. An Instagram bio is built for discovery and has almost no room. An EPK sits between them: built for one specific reader making one specific decision, so it stays to a single page or screen and leads with exactly what that decision needs.

Frequently asked questions

Who actually reads an EPK?

Venue bookers, festival submission reviewers, blog and playlist curators, and radio music directors — almost always skimming dozens or hundreds of submissions, so a one-page, scannable format is the point, not a limitation.

How is an EPK different from a website or Instagram bio?

A website is built for fans and can be as deep as you like; an EPK is built for a gatekeeper making a fast yes/no decision, so it stays to one page or screen and leads with exactly what that decision needs: who you sound like, what you've done, and how to reach you.

Do I need professional photos and press quotes before making one?

No. A clean phone photo and no press coverage yet is a normal, complete first EPK — the generator simply omits any section you leave blank rather than showing a placeholder. Update it as you get better photos and your first write-up.

Build one now →

No warranty. This page is informational, describing common practice among independent musicians and the people who book and cover them — not a rule any venue, festival, or publication is bound by. Confirm what a specific submission actually wants before sending it.
